summary: Specifies the use of Curve25519 and Curve448 key exchange methods in the Secure Shell protocol. These elliptic curve methods let the two sides of an SSH connection agree on a shared secret.

eli5.summary: Two people can agree on a secret number while talking in public. This adds two modern ways, using Curve25519 and Curve448, for SSH to do it.

questions: how does ssh key exchange work with curve25519
subtitle: Two elliptic curve key exchange methods for SSH, built on Curve25519 and Curve448.

tldr.problem: SSH needs a way for client and server to agree on a shared secret. Curve25519 key exchange was already deployed under a private name in libssh and OpenSSH but was not standardized, and Curve448 had no SSH method.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers "curve25519-sha256" and "curve448-sha512". They reuse the ECDH messages and exchange hash of RFC 5656 but use the X25519 and X448 functions, with a different encoding for public values and the shared secret.
tldr.outcome: Curve25519 with SHA-256 is the preferred choice at about 128 bits of security. Curve448 with SHA-512 is offered as a hedge at about 224 bits.

today: RFC 8731 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It is not obsoleted and has no updates listed.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SSH key exchange protocol in RFC 4253 supports an extensible set of methods. RFC 5656 defines how elliptic curves fit into that framework, and this RFC reuses the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) message definitions from Section 7.1 of that document. Other parts of RFC 5656, such as ECMQV and ECDSA, are not considered here.

The Curve25519 method with SHA-256 is equivalent to the privately defined algorithm curve25519-sha256@libssh.org, which at the time of publication was implemented and widely deployed in libssh and OpenSSH. The Curve448 method is similar but uses SHA-512.
sections.eli5: A version of this trick was already in use under a private name. This RFC makes it official and adds a bigger, tougher sibling.

sections.title: The Key Exchange Methods
sections.content:
The procedure is similar to the ECDH method in Section 4 of RFC 5656, with a different wire encoding for public values and for the final shared secret. Public ephemeral keys travel as standard SSH strings. The protocol flow, the SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT and SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY messages, and the structure of the exchange hash are identical to RFC 5656.

The registered method names are curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512. They perform Diffie-Hellman using the functions X25519 and X448 from RFC 7748. Public keys are strings of 32 bytes for Curve25519 and 56 bytes for Curve448. The hash is SHA-256 for the first and SHA-512 for the second.
sections.eli5: Both sides swap a public number, mix it with a private one, and end up with the same secret. The messages are the same ones SSH already used for the older elliptic curve version.

sections.title: Checks and Aborts
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD compute X25519 and X448 using the algorithms in RFC 7748. When they do, they MUST check whether the computed shared secret is the all-zero value and abort if so. Alternative implementations SHOULD abort when either side's input forces the shared secret to one of a small set of values.

Clients and servers MUST also abort if a received public key is not the expected length. An abort means disconnecting the session with SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT, and it SHOULD use the reason SSH_DISCONNECT_KEY_EXCHANGE_FAILED. No further validation is required beyond what RFC 7748 describes.
sections.eli5: If the other side sends a number that is the wrong size, or one that would make the secret something obvious, SSH hangs up instead of carrying on.

sections.title: Shared Secret Encoding
sections.content:
The shared secret K is defined in RFC 4253 and RFC 5656 as an integer encoded as an mpint. Curve25519 and Curve448 instead produce a binary string X of 32 or 56 bytes. This RFC converts X into K by reading the octets as an unsigned fixed-length integer in network byte order. This differs from the conversion in RFC 5656, but only for the methods in this document.

Inside X25519 and X448 the values are encoded as fixed-length unsigned little-endian byte strings, as RFC 7748 says. The bytes are reinterpreted as a big-endian integer K only when passed to the ECDH function in SSH. K is then encoded as a variable-length signed mpint and fed, with other data, to the hash function to generate encryption keys.
sections.eli5: The secret comes out as a row of bytes, and SSH has to read that row in a particular direction to turn it into a number. This section says which way, so both sides agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4251, RFC 5656 and RFC 7748 are inherited. Curve25519 with SHA-256 provides strong (about 128 bits) security and is efficient on a wide range of architectures. Curve448 with SHA-512 provides about 224 bits, but has not received the same cryptographic review, and is slower. It is offered as a hedge against unforeseen analytical advances.

The way the mpint is encoded before hashing, adding or removing zero bytes, raises the potential for a side-channel attack that could reveal the length of what is hashed. That would leak the most significant bit of the secret or show when the most significant bytes are zero. For backwards-compatibility reasons, the authors decided not to address this.

The RFC names curve25519-sha256 as the preferred choice, and suggests implementing curve448-sha512 in case more than 128 bits of strength is ever required.
sections.eli5: The smaller curve is the everyday choice and is strong. The bigger one is a spare in case the smaller one is someday cracked. The authors also admit one tiny leak they chose not to fix.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512 to the "Key Exchange Method Names" registry for SSH, which was created in Section 4.10 of RFC 4250.
sections.eli5: The official list of SSH secret-agreeing methods now includes both names.
